pron_note: Also heard dil-uh-TAHNT, stress on the last syllable. Plural often dilettanti (dil-uh-TAHN-tee).
means:
Someone who dabbles in an art or subject **for pleasure and without serious commitment** — enough knowledge to talk at a party, not enough to do the work.

The sting is not incompetence but **pretension**: an *amateur* simply isn't paid, and can be devoted and excellent; a **dilettante** performs expertise he hasn't earned. Calling someone a dilettante says they're playing at it. As an adjective — *a dilettante interest in physics* — it means shallow, easily dropped.
trap: **dilettante ≠ dilatory.** *Dilatory* (**DIL-uh-tor-ee**) means **slow, delaying, dragging your feet** — a dilatory tenant hasn't paid rent. Same opening syllable, unrelated roots. The dilettante does it badly; the dilatory man hasn't got round to doing it at all.
trick_line: A **dilettante** is a **debutante** of the arts — same *-tante* ending, same instinct: turn up for the party, leave before the work.
trick_unpack: The rhyme carries the contempt, which is the part the definition alone misses.
sentences: Critics dismissed him as a **dilettante** — three exhibitions, four abandoned novels, and no discernible craft behind any of them.
Don't ask me, I'm a total **dilettante** — I've watched two YouTube videos on fermentation and now I own a crock.
etymology:
Italian **dilettante** = *"one who delights (in something),"* from Latin **delectāre**, *to delight*. It began as a compliment — an eighteenth-century gentleman who loved painting or music without earning from it — and curdled into an insult once *professional* became the word of praise.

That root is still visible in **delight, delectable, delectation** — which is the memory key: a dilettante is in it purely for the **delight**, and quits the moment it stops being fun.
one_line: Dabbler who plays at an art without serious commitment.
